title: Stop Treating GitHub Like Google Drive 💀
description: Your GitHub profile is more than a place to dump code. Let's make it something people actually enjoy exploring.
author: spideythedev

content.text: Let's be honest. Some developers treat GitHub like a storage device. Create a repository, upload some files, write a README that says 'My Project', and disappear. 😭
And honestly? I get it. When you're building something, the last thing you want to do is spend another hour writing documentation. You just want to see your project working.

But here's something worth thinking about: GitHub isn't just where your code lives. It's where people can discover your work, understand your ideas, learn from your experiments and even collaborate with you.
Your repository is someone's first impression

Imagine someone discovering your project. They open the repository and see 47 files, absolutely no explanation, five different folders named test-final-new-final, and a README that contains one sentence.
What are they supposed to do? Hire a detective? 💀
A good repository should answer a few simple questions without making visitors work for it:
What is this project? Why does it exist? What can it do? How can I use it? And where can I learn more?
1. Give your README some personality
Your README is usually the first thing people read. Don't waste that opportunity with something like 'This is a project made using JavaScript.'
Explain the actual idea. Show what makes it interesting. Add a screenshot if the project has a visual interface. Include installation instructions and a small example.
You don't need a 900-line README either. Just make it useful.

content.code:
# Project Name

A short explanation of what this thing actually does.

## Features
- Something useful
- Something interesting
- Something that makes people go 'wait, that's cool'

## Getting Started

Installation and usage instructions go here.

## License
MIT

content.text: 2. Your commit history tells a story
Compare these two commit messages:

content.code:
update
fixed stuff
final final
changes

fix: prevent blank screen on refresh
feat: add markdown code highlighting
docs: improve installation guide
refactor: simplify post loading

content.text: Which one would you rather read? Exactly.
Good commit messages make your project easier to understand later. They also make collaboration less painful. Your future self will thank you. Probably with fewer swear words.
3. Make your project easy to try
If your project is a website, provide a live demo when possible. If it's a library, provide a tiny usage example. If it's a CLI, show the commands and expected output.
Don't make someone clone a repository, install 27 dependencies, configure three environment variables and sacrifice a weekend just to understand what your project does.
A quick preview can make a huge difference.
4. Don't forget the small details
A few things are easy to overlook, but they make repositories much better:

Use a .gitignore file so you don't accidentally upload node_modules, build output or local configuration. Add a LICENSE so people know how they can use your code. Document environment variables without exposing actual secrets. Keep your folder structure understandable. Remove abandoned experiments when they only create confusion.
And please, don't commit your API keys. That's not open source. That's an invitation. 😭
5. Your GitHub profile deserves attention too
Pin projects you're genuinely proud of. Keep your profile README interesting. Add descriptions to your repositories. Make sure the projects you showcase are actually understandable.
You don't need 500 repositories. Three well-explained projects can be much more interesting than 100 unfinished ones.
Also, don't build projects just to make your contribution graph look like a Christmas tree. Build things because you want to build them.
6. Open source isn't just about writing code
This is something I think more developers should understand. You don't have to be an expert programmer to contribute to open source.
You can improve documentation, report bugs, reproduce issues, suggest features, review instructions or help other contributors understand a project.
A good project isn't built by code alone. It's built by people who care enough to make it better.
So, what should you do now?
Open one of your repositories. Pick a project you actually care about. Read its README as if you've never seen it before.
Can you understand what it does? Can you run it? Are the instructions clear? Does it have a proper license? Is the code reasonably organized?
Fix one thing today. You don't need to redesign your entire GitHub profile overnight.
Build things people can explore, understand and use. Don't just upload code and call it a day.
Anyway, that's it. Now go check your repositories. And if you find a folder called final-final-v2-real, we need to talk. 😂
